Algorithm Theoretical Basis Document

Joint Multi-Atmosphere Bin Retrieval for Along-Slit Keystone/Smile Correction

A state-space, nearest-bin joint estimator that recovers a per-along-slit-position CO2 field from a keystone- and smile-distorted GeoCarb-like focal plane, in place of native's one-atmosphere-per-detector-row assumption.

Status: Phase 0–3 diagnostic, pre–whole-slit validation Instrument: GeoCarb FPA2 (simulated) Scene: noise-free, realistic along-slit CO₂ Parent study: KEYSTONE_SMILE_BIAS_PLAN.md §11p

1Purpose and Scope

Native GeoCarb-style Level 2 retrieval fits one atmospheric state per detector row. Because the real focal plane exhibits keystone (wavelength-dependent spatial magnification) and smile (position-dependent spectral curvature), a single row's own 1024 columns do not sample one true along-slit position — they sample a range of positions that widens with keystone amplitude. Fitting one atmosphere to that spliced mixture systematically dilutes any real, spatially localized signal: a simulated CO₂ point source at high keystone (FPA2 row 910, rows_crossed ≈ 9.3) recovers only 44% of its true peak-to-background enhancement under native retrieval, versus 99% for an idealized undistorted instrument (KEYSTONE_SMILE_BIAS_PLAN.md §11p).

This document describes a joint, multi-atmosphere alternative: partition the along-slit coordinate into G discrete bins, assign every real detector pixel to its nearest bin by its own exact along-slit position, and solve for all G atmospheric states simultaneously against every real pixel in a neighborhood — never interpolating or blending measured radiances. The method is deliberately conservative in one respect and permissive in another: it reuses the instrument forward model (ForwardModel, ILS convolution, spatial PSF) exactly as built for native retrieval, and it reuses gert.retrieval.StateVector's scalar gas-transform machinery per bin — but it does not reuse GERTRetrieval itself, whose single-atmosphere architecture does not generalize to a block-sparse multi-state estimate (§7).

Scope: this document covers the G-bin CO₂-only formulation validated on a synthetic two-state test (Phase 0) and a realistic single-hot-spot diagnostic (Phase 1–3). It does not yet cover a whole-slit sweep, added measurement noise, jointly-retrieved nuisance gases, or a validated averaging-kernel resolution characterization — each is listed explicitly in §10.

2Terminology

Two layers of terms are used throughout: physical/geometric quantities that exist independent of any retrieval design choice, and modeling quantities that are choices made in building this specific estimator. Conflating the two — in particular treating a bin as though it were a row — is the single most common source of confusion working with this method.

Physical / geometric layer

TermDefinition
sceneThe true, continuous physical radiance field along the slit — a function radiance(η) → spectrum. Reality itself, independent of how the instrument samples or distorts it.
η (eta)Normalized along-slit position, η ∈ [−1, 1] — a physical coordinate for “where along the slit,” independent of detector row or column. xkm = η × SLIT_HALF_KM is the same quantity in physical distance.
pixelOne detector element at row i, column j. Has its own exact true (η(i,j), ν(i,j)) from the real ground-test dispersion polynomials, and one measured/predicted radiance A[i,j].
footprintThe along-slit domain that physically contributes to a given pixel's — or a given retrieval's — measured value. Widened by keystone (a row's own columns sweep a range of η), by the spatial PSF (neighboring rows' true radiance blends in), and, for a regularized joint retrieval, by the prior's own correlation length (§8).
rowOne horizontal line of 1024 pixels sharing detector row index i. Not a single along-slit position — its footprint is a range of η, which is the root mechanism behind the dilution bias this method addresses.

Retrieval / modeling layer

TermDefinition
binA segment of the η-axis, with one representative center, to which a single atmospheric state is assigned in the joint state vector. A discretization choice, not a physical unit — real pixels from many different rows may be assigned to one bin, and a single row's pixels may be split across several bins (§5).
bin assignmentThe map from a pixel's own exact η(i,j) to its nearest bin center. State-space only — never interpolates or blends measured radiance values (§4).
neighborhoodThe contiguous row range [row_min, row_max] over which one joint solve runs — a chosen window size, not a physical unit.
atmosphere / stateThe physical quantity assigned to each bin. In general a full AtmosphericProfile; in the current implementation, a scalar co2_scale multiplying a bin-specific local prior atmosphere.

3Physical Basis: the Known Distortion Operator

Unlike a generic ill-posed deconvolution problem, the distortion here is known exactly. Detector-plane position maps to (wavelength, along-slit position) via ground-test-calibrated polynomials, xy_to_wavelength_slit(fpa, col, row) → (λ, s), validated against real GeoCarb ground-test data (KEYSTONE_SMILE_BIAS_PLAN.md §9). Three effects compose to determine a pixel's true sample position:

EffectCharacterConsequence for one row's footprint
keystoneSpatial magnification varies with wavelengthA row's own columns sweep a range of η that grows with keystone amplitude — measured by rows_crossed(fpa, row), an endpoint-to-endpoint difference in row-equivalent units.
smileSpectral position curves quadratically with ηCan produce real within-row structure even where rows_crossed ≈ 0 — FPA2's row 25 (endpoint-null) still shows 0.63 km peak-to-peak internal η excursion.
spatial PSFAlong-slit (row-to-row) blur, ground-test-measured ~1.5 px FWHM, applied via gaussian_blur_rowsGenuinely mixes true radiance across neighboring rows — the one place cross-row mixing in the forward model is physically correct rather than an artifact.

Because the distortion operator is known rather than estimated, this is a classical (if non-separable) forward-modeling problem, not a blind deconvolution: every pixel's exact (η, ν) is computable in closed form, and the estimation task is choosing what atmospheric state to assign at each along-slit position given that known mapping.

4Forward Model Formulation

State-space only, never radiance-space

The single governing rule, carried over unchanged from every other pipeline in this study: a pixel's predicted radiance is computed by running the radiative transfer model once, at that pixel's own exact η, then convolving at that pixel's own exact ν. If two along-slit states are relevant to one column's neighborhood, the correct place to interpolate is the atmospheric state itself — never the already-computed spectra. This is not a stylistic preference: bilinearly interpolating already-rendered pixel radiances is precisely the mechanism identified as the dominant bias source in this whole investigation (KEYSTONE_SMILE_BIAS_PLAN.md §9l/§9m, an approximately −62 ppm CO₂ bias from the rectify pipeline, present even on a spatially uniform scene). The joint bin estimator avoids it by construction: nearest-bin assignment picks exactly one bin's own, independently-computed spectrum for every pixel — no blending, ever.

Pipeline

5Bin Definition and Placement

A bin is not a row

Because bin assignment operates per pixel on η(i,j), not per row, a bin corresponds to a set of whole contiguous rows only in the limit where a row's own footprint is much narrower than one bin. Wherever a row's footprint is comparable to or wider than bin width — i.e. wherever keystone is large — that row's own columns are split across multiple bins. Figure 2 shows this directly and quantitatively for the row used in the worked example (§9): at row 910 (rows_crossed = 9.3), the row's own 1024 columns cross three bin boundaries under the G=15 placement used in §9 — that row alone contributes real pixels to four separate bins, un-splicing within one row exactly what keystone spliced together there. This is the specific mechanism that lets the joint estimator do something a per-row (or coarser per-row-group) retrieval structurally cannot.

Placement: uniform vs. pixel-density

Two rules for choosing the G bin centers were implemented and compared:

SchemeRuleRationale
uniformnp.linspace over the neighborhood's η rangeBaseline; bin density constant regardless of local distortion.
pixel‑densityBin centers at evenly-spaced quantiles of the actual per-pixel η distribution in the neighborhoodWherever keystone is large, more rows' footprints overlap a given η interval, so real pixel density is genuinely higher there — both because native's dilution problem is worse there (need) and because more independent pixels support a finer bin there (data support).

An earlier version of the pixel-density scheme used rows_crossed(fpa, row) as an indirect per-row proxy for this density, routed through each row's own center-column η. It required an explicit floor to handle a near-null row whose real internal wiggle (smile-driven curvature, not keystone's own endpoint measure) reads as zero keystone by the endpoint-difference definition. Placing bins directly at quantiles of the real per-pixel η distribution (pixel_density_bin_centers) supersedes it: no proxy, no floor, and it captures footprint overlap from both keystone and smile automatically, since it measures actual data density rather than inferring it from one geometric quantity.

Scope of this test

Rows 890–935 sit entirely within FPA2's high-keystone regime (rows_crossed spans only 9.09→9.55 across the window) — there is little keystone contrast within it for pixel-density weighting to respond to differently than uniform spacing. The scheme's design goal — concentrating resolution where keystone is large and starving it where keystone is small — is not strongly exercised by this particular window; it would be by a neighborhood spanning from near FPA2's keystone-null row (~25) through a high-keystone region. That comparison has not yet been run (§10).

6Joint Estimation

State vector and observation model

The state is x = [x1…xG], one co2_scale per bin. Every bin's nuisance gases (H₂O, CH₄, CO, surface pressure) are held at their own local true value, als.atmosphere_at(x_km_bin) — the same function that generates the real scene's per-position truth — rather than jointly retrieved (§8 discusses the resulting idealization). The observation vector y is every real pixel's measured radiance in the neighborhood, raveled; the forward operator F(x) is exactly the pipeline in Figure 1.

Regularized Gauss–Newton update

This is standard Rodgers-form optimal estimation, generalized from one atmosphere's several gas/nuisance parameters (as GERTRetrieval already does) to G copies of one gas's scale factor:

Rodgers update
Δx = (KTSy−1K + Sa−1)−1 (KTSy−1·resid − Sa−1·(x−xa))
Prior precision — first-difference Tikhonov smoothness
Sa−1 = γ·(LTL) + σabs−2I

where L is the (G−1)×G first-difference operator (Lk,k = −1, Lk,k+1 = 1), so LTL is the standard discrete graph Laplacian penalizing differences between adjacent bins. The σabs term is a loose absolute floor that keeps the system well-posed against the Laplacian's own null space (a uniform shift of every bin together). This entire solve is joint — one linear system per iteration for all G bins — not G independent per-bin fits smoothed together afterward; a bin with too few of its own pixels to independently constrain is still correctly constrained by its neighbors within the same solve, never separately estimated and then blended.

γ is an assumed correlation length, not a numerical convenience

The regularization strength encodes a real claim about how correlated the true CO₂ field is at the scale of one bin spacing. Two limits are worth stating precisely:

  • If the true field were spatially white below the bin scale, any γ > 0 is actively wrong — it pulls a bin's estimate toward neighbors that have no real relationship to it, reproducing a version of the same dilution bias this method exists to fix, now sourced from the prior instead of from row-splicing.
  • If the true field is smooth relative to bin spacing, a correlation-aware prior is legitimate information, not a fudge — it lets the joint solve extract more from the ensemble of measurements than any single one could give alone, the same logic that justifies any optimal-estimation prior.

A sensitivity check over γ ∈ {0.3, 3.0, 30} — a 100× range — left the worked example's capture fraction essentially unchanged (81.7%, 81.7%, 81.8% for uniform bins). This reflects the specific test scene's own smoothness (a Gaussian hot spot, width ≈ 9–10 km) more than it demonstrates general insensitivity to γ; a sharper or genuinely uncorrelated synthetic truth has not yet been tested against the same sweep (§10).

7Algorithm Implementation

Reusable, unmodified pieces vs. new code, and their location:

ComponentRoleLocation
StateVector.gas_scaling / .applyScalar co2_scale → modified AtmosphericProfile, per bin. Reused unmodified.gert/retrieval.py
ForwardModelRadiative transfer for one atmosphere. Reused unmodified.gert/forward_model.py
nearest_bin_sceneG-bin generalization of edge_scene; hard nearest-bin assignment, no interpolation.geocarb_gert/focalplane.py
predict_neighborhoodForward operator: image()'s own per-row loop, restricted to a padded row window. Bit-identical to image() on the requested rows (validated).geocarb_gert/gd_render.py
make_spectrum_fn / build_forwardPer-bin spectrum evaluation with caching (only changed bins recomputed per iteration); assembles F(x).scripts/gd_joint_block_retrieve.py
gauss_newton_regularizedStandalone Rodgers-form GN/OE loop. New code — not a gert modification, not GERTRetrieval.scripts/gd_joint_block_retrieve.py
uniform_bin_centers / pixel_density_bin_centersBin placement rules (§5).scripts/gd_joint_block_diagnostics.py
bin_assign / per_bin_chi2Per-pixel bin assignment and per-bin reduced-χ² diagnostic (§8).scripts/gd_joint_block_diagnostics.py
gd_toy_joint_g2_test.pyPhase 0 synthetic two-state validation (§9 references its result).scripts/

What was deliberately not reused: GERTRetrieval. Direct inspection of gert/retrieval.py found StateVector.apply() maps onto exactly one AtmosphericProfile, GERTRetrieval.__init__ takes exactly one ForwardModel/StateVector pair, and its Gauss–Newton step is not factored out separately from that single-atmosphere plumbing. Subclassing or monkey-patching to fake a multi-atmosphere state was judged more fragile than a small standalone solver built on the pieces that do generalize cleanly.

8Error Characterization

For an audience accustomed to OCO-2's Rodgers-form error budget — smoothing error, forward model parameter error, and retrieval noise — the useful framing is: native retrieval's dilution bias is an extreme, uncharacterized smoothing error. A single-atmosphere-per-row fit implicitly assumes an averaging kernel of the identity — no averaging at all — when the real footprint says otherwise. The joint bin estimator's whole contribution is to make that averaging kernel wider than the identity on purpose, and, eventually, to characterize it rather than ignore it.

8.1 — Quantization (finite G)

Representing a continuously-varying true field with G discrete states introduces a residual proportional to local curvature (Figure 3) — largest at the peak, negligible on smooth background. In the worked example, per-bin reduced χ² is 2–3 orders of magnitude larger for bins spanning the hot spot's steep flank than for background bins, directly confirming this is the dominant residual source rather than, say, a wavelength-registration error (both truth and model are evaluated at identical pixel wavenumbers, so registration mismatch is structurally impossible here).

8.2 — The resolution floor is not just bin width

A bin's actual footprint — the along-slit domain its one retrieved value represents an average over — has two contributors, only one of which shrinks with G: (a) bin assignment width, which the modeler controls, and (b) the spatial PSF's own ~1.5 px blur, which is already irreversibly baked into every pixel's measured value before bin assignment ever happens. Shrinking bins below the PSF's own footprint does not recover additional true resolution — it chops an already-smoothed signal into more, increasingly redundant labels. This is the physical content behind “underdetermined as G grows” and the reason a smoothness prior is structurally necessary at large G, not merely convenient.

The rigorous tool for characterizing this — not yet built — is the generalized averaging kernel A = (KTSy−1K + Sa−1)−1KTSy−1K, exactly analogous to the vertical averaging kernels OCO-2's own L2 full-physical retrieval reports, applied here in the along-slit spatial dimension instead of the vertical.

8.3 — Point-sample vs. footprint-integrated forward model

Every pixel, in both the synthetic truth generator and this forward model, is evaluated as an exact point sample of radiance(η) — there is no explicit integration over a pixel's own finite footprint width in either. A Taylor expansion shows the resulting error is second order: negligible where the true scene is locally linear, and systematically overstating peak amplitude wherever the scene has real curvature (a concave-down peak's true footprint-average is lower than its center point value). Because both sides of every residual use the same approximation, this does not distort the comparisons in this study — but it means even “undistorted”'s own reported ~99% capture (KEYSTONE_SMILE_BIAS_PLAN.md §11p) may be somewhat optimistic relative to what any physically real detector, with finite pixels, could ever measure. Not yet quantified (§10).

8.4 — Idealizations specific to this diagnostic

  • Nuisance gases (H₂O, CH₄, CO, surface pressure) are fixed to each bin's own local true value rather than jointly retrieved — isolating the CO₂ bin-splicing question from a separate, larger free-nuisance-state engineering problem.
  • Sy−1 is a simple uniform relative weighting (1/mean(y)²), not the instrument's real photon-noise model — acceptable on a still-noise-free scene where the limiting factor is model mismatch (§8.1), not noise-weighted averaging.
  • All results in this document use the no-noise convention established throughout this study; no realized-noise Monte Carlo sweep has been run (§10).

9Worked Example: FPA2 Hot Spot at High Keystone

Neighborhood rows 890–935 (46 rows), G=15, γ=3.0, the same realistic no-noise FPA2 scene behind results/gd_joint_fpa2.pkl and every prior comparison in this study. Peak-enhancement capture, native's own §11p metric, scores the retrieved rise between row 910 (true hot spot) and row 880 (background) against the true rise:

MethodCaptureNote
native44%One atmosphere per row (KEYSTONE_SMILE_BIAS_PLAN.md §11p)
undistorted99%Idealized, no keystone/smile (upper bound; see §8.3 caveat)
trace-and-select84.9%Scattered real pixels within 0.5 km of target η, single-atmosphere fit
joint block, uniform bins81.7%G=15, mean per-bin χ² = 2.58×10−8, min pixel count/bin = 269
joint block, pixel-density bins90.9%G=15, mean per-bin χ² = 1.87×10−8, min pixel count/bin = 890

Both joint-block variants converged in 2 Gauss–Newton iterations (~80 s wall time). The G=1 control — a single shared atmosphere fit to the identical pixels — recovered 413.77 ppm, far below the true peak (416.98 ppm) and close to the window's own background, the same structural dilution native exhibits, reproduced here as the required control (Phase 0's own success criterion, §7).

Reading this result

The joint block closes most of the gap between native (44%) and undistorted (99%), and is comparable to — not yet clearly better than — trace-and-select's much cheaper per-row selection (84.9%). At one hot spot, with nuisance parameters idealized away on the joint-block side, that comparison does not yet justify the larger engineering investment of a fully free per-bin nuisance state. A whole-slit, head-to-head sweep against trace-and-select is the natural next step (§10).
